title: Letting go
hook: renunciation as the relief of wanting less, not grim denial

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cowherd in autumn, and your line, guard then rest. Once the guarding was done, did you let yourself rest under the tree for a minute? Day three hundred sixty-two.
screen: `THE COWHERD IN AUTUMN — GUARD, THEN REST.`

segments.voice: Moving day. The twelfth box comes down the stairs, and inside are chargers for phones nobody in the house has owned in years. The whole box goes in the donation bin, and something odd can happen. The shoulders come down. The body feels lighter, and not only in the arms. Nobody would call that grim. Nobody would call it a sacrifice. It's closer to relief. That, in miniature, is the first thought in the Buddha's good pile, the one from two days ago, and its usual English translation can mislead. Today: letting go.
screen: `THE TWELFTH BOX.` → `DROPPED AT THE BIN.` → `THE SHOULDERS COME DOWN.`

segments.voice: The word is nekkhamma, usually translated renunciation, and renunciation sounds like a monk in a cold cell refusing soup. In the suttas the word can point to going forth, leaving home to become a monk or nun. But it also names a thought anyone can have: the thought of putting something down. In the sutta of the two kinds of thought, the Buddha remembers sorting his thinking, before his awakening, into two piles. In one: sensual wanting, ill will, harming. In the other: letting go, goodwill, not harming. Letting go comes first in the good pile. Here's the honest part. In another sutta, a householder named Tapussa tells Ananda that letting go looks, to people like him, like a cliff edge. Ananda takes him to the Buddha, whose answer is candid. Before his awakening, he says, he too thought renunciation was good, yet his heart didn't leap at it. It only did once he had truly seen the trouble that wanting brings, and tasted the ease of not wanting. So the tradition doesn't say grit your teeth. It says look closely until the relief becomes real to you. The Dhammapada frames it as a trade, in Max Müller's words: "If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great." And nekkhamma isn't only for monks. Theravada tradition counts it among the perfections, and some lay people practice it in small doses, keeping eight precepts on an observance day. Less, chosen freely, can feel like more room.
screen: `NEKKHAMMA: THE THOUGHT OF PUTTING DOWN.` · `FIRST IN THE GOOD PILE.` · `TAPUSSA: IT LOOKS LIKE A CLIFF.` · `LOOK UNTIL THE RELIEF IS REAL.` · then, large: `THE RELIEF OF LESS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you want right now. Not a big life want. Something small and live: the next snack, the reply to a message, a purchase waiting in a cart. Notice how the wanting sits in the body, a lean forward, a little tightness somewhere. Now, just for these two minutes, put it down. You can pick it up later if you choose. Watch what the body does when you set it down. If there's any relief, rest in it. The bell holds the time.
Nekkhamma. Letting go, renunciation: the thought of putting something down, first in the good pile, felt as relief rather than loss.
Your line: the relief of less. Today, put down one want, a purchase, a second helping, an argument you were planning to win, and notice how you feel an hour later. Day three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Buddhists practice letting go in small doses: on observance days lay people may keep eight precepts, skipping the evening meal and entertainment, and in some Theravada countries men may ordain as monks for a short time.

fork.setup: you're Tapussa, a householder. you've told Ananda that letting go looks like a cliff edge to you. what does the Buddha say?
options: it's easy; you just aren't trying.
he felt the same, until he saw the trouble in wanting.
fork.reveal: in AN 9.41 the Buddha says that before his awakening his heart didn't leap at renunciation either; it did once he had seen the drawbacks of sensual wanting and tasted the ease of letting go.

original.note: Pali nekkhamma (Sanskrit naiṣkramya): letting go, renunciation, from the same family as going forth.

trapdoor: what you thought: renunciation means grim self-denial.
what it means: the thought of putting something down, and the relief that comes with it.
what a scholar hears: the Pali Text Society dictionary links nekkhamma to going out, the root of going forth, while noting that in use it sits close to being free of sensual desire.
